views.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: We should enter the G20 meeting with Xi as a genuine negotiation, using the scheduled January 1 escalation of the $200B list (10% to 25%) as leverage rather than prematurely triggering it. Hold the current tariff posture in place, signal openness to scaling back if Beijing delivers concrete, verifiable commitments on IP/tech-transfer and purchases, and avoid any new escalation that would spook already-stressed markets and further alienate farm-belt constituents. This is a moment to negotiate from strength, not to overplay our hand.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The dispute is not an existential threat to US interests; we initiated the Section 301 action, hold ~$250B of Chinese imports under tariffs (timeline: Lists 1-2 at 25%, List 3 at 10% effective Sept 24), and China is the more exposed party — so the terrain is favorable and the reading is a mild opportunity (threat_score -0.3). But it is not a clean -0.5/-1.0 opportunity because the costs are real and rising: Chinese retaliation has hit the soybean/pork farm belt (CNN: prices tanked, farm values down ~$200k, a political liability that already shaped the midterms), and US macro shows accumulating stress — corporate credit spreads widened (Moody's Baa yield up to ~5.18% from ~4.8-4.9), the Fed is tightening (fed funds 2.20%, up ~20bp over the window), CPI is running near 3%, a strong dollar (broad index ~115) and the October equity selloff/VIX spike point to fragility (CBS/Deutsche Bank). These costs argue against maximal escalation. The action stance is negotiate (action_score ~0.0): the Nov 1 Trump-Xi call with a positive tone and agreement to meet at the G20, plus Kudlow's stated willingness to hold off and potentially scale back if talks succeed, provides a concrete off-ramp; with the Democrats taking the House in January, unilateral trade actions will draw heavier congressional scrutiny, making a negotiated settlement that returns farm-belt exports and calms markets the least-cost path. Escalating now would risk the opposite of our intent — inviting further retaliation and compounding domestic economic and political stress — so we hold firm at the table rather than pulling the trigger.
key_factors: US holds offensive initiative with ~$250B of Chinese imports under Section 301 tariffs
Nov 1 Trump-Xi call + agreement to meet at G20; Kudlow signals willingness to scale back if talks succeed
China retaliation hitting US farm belt (soybeans/pork), a midterm political liability
US macro showing stress: widening Baa credit spreads (~5.18%), Fed tightening, ~3% CPI, strong dollar, October market selloff
Democrats won House in Nov 6 midterms; greater congressional scrutiny of trade policy ahead
January 1 escalation of $200B list (10%->25%) available as leverage, not yet triggered

sources_cited.excerpt: Trump and Xi hold a phone call focused on trade; agree to meet at the G20 in Argentina.
List 3 takes effect at 10%. China imposes retaliatory tariffs (5-10%) on ~$60B of US goods. Combined US Section 301 coverage now ~$250B.
Trump directs USTR to finalize List 3: 10% tariffs on ~$200B effective Sept 24, scheduled to rise to 25% on Jan 1, 2019.
Moody's Baa corporate bond yield rose to ~5.18% (from ~4.8%) over the window — credit stress widening.
Federal funds rate 2.20% at decision date, up ~20bp over the window; Fed tightening.
Trump-Xi 'long and very good conversation'; Kudlow: hold off on further tariffs and may scale back existing ones if talks succeed.
Dismal October wiped out most of the year's market gains; elevated VIX; Democratic House means Congress plays a bigger role in trade policy.
Soybean/pork growers 'collateral damage'; farms losing over $200k in value as commodity prices slump amid the China dispute.
